_about: Secret Shield patterns, shared by the daemon (secret_shield.py) and the git hook fallback (scripts/secret-shield/scanner.mjs). Keep regexes valid in both Python and JavaScript: no inline flags (use "flags": "i"), numbered groups only. "group" is the capture group holding the secret (0 = the whole match). Mirror allowlist changes in .gitleaks.toml.

rules.label: a private key (SSH, TLS or signing key)
a Discord webhook link (anyone with it can post as the webhook)
a password, token or key written into a file

allow.description: Fake credentials used on purpose by Orion's secret-filter tests (made of alphabet runs, hunter2 and so on)
Orion's own tripwire decoys (apps/daemon/tripwires.py): every bait value carries the orntw marker

_after: After rotating: the old value is still inside the git history. Rotating is what protects you, because the old value stops working. Rewriting history (git filter-repo) only hides it, and anyone who already copied the repo keeps it. If you want it removed anyway, ask Orion to plan it; rewriting published history waits for your approval.
Move the new value into apps/daemon/.env (that file is never committed) instead of putting it in code.
Run "Orion, is anything secret in my repos?" again to confirm the repo is clean.
openai: Find the leaked key and press Revoke (or Delete). It stops working straight away.
Press "Create new secret key" and copy it.
Paste it into apps/daemon/.env as OPENAI_API_KEY=... and restart Orion.
Check https://platform.openai.com/usage for any spending you don't recognise.
anthropic: Find the leaked key, open its menu and choose Delete (or Disable).
Press "Create Key" and copy the new key.
Paste it into apps/daemon/.env as ANTHROPIC_API_KEY=... and restart Orion.
Check the Usage page in the console for anything you don't recognise.
github: Find the leaked token and press Delete (or Revoke).
Create a new token with only the permissions you need and a short expiry.
Put the new token where the old one was used (for example gh auth login, or an Actions secret), never in code.
Look at https://github.com/settings/security-log for anything you didn't do.
gitlab: Open GitLab, then Preferences > Access tokens.
Create a new one with only the scopes you need and put it in .env.
discord: Open https://discord.com/developers/applications and pick your bot's application.
Go to Bot and press "Reset Token". The old token stops working at once.
Copy the new token into apps/daemon/.env as DISCORD_TOKEN=... and restart Orion.
Check your servers' audit logs for messages or changes the bot didn't make.
discord_webhook: In Discord, open the channel's settings > Integrations > Webhooks.
Delete the leaked webhook (anyone with the link could post as it).
Create a new webhook and keep its link in .env, not in code.
telegram: In Telegram, open a chat with @BotFather.
Send /revoke, pick your bot, and BotFather gives you a new token. The old one stops working.
Put the new token into apps/daemon/.env as TELEGRAM_BOT_TOKEN=... and restart Orion.
slack: Open https://api.slack.com/apps and pick the app.
For a token: OAuth & Permissions > revoke or rotate it. For a webhook: Incoming Webhooks > remove it and add a new one.
stripe: Press "Roll key" on the leaked key and choose to expire the old one now.
Put the new key in .env and check recent payments and payouts for anything odd.
aws: Open the AWS console > IAM > Users > the user > Security credentials.
Deactivate the leaked access key, then delete it.
Create a new access key only if you still need one, and store it in .env or the AWS credentials file.
Check Billing and CloudTrail for activity you didn't start (leaked AWS keys are often used for crypto mining within minutes).
google: Find the key and press Regenerate key (or delete it and create a new one).
Add restrictions to the new key (which APIs and which apps may use it) and store it in .env.
huggingface: Open the leaked token's menu and choose Invalidate and refresh (or Delete).
npm: Open https://www.npmjs.com/settings/~/tokens (or run: npm token list).
Delete the leaked token (or run: npm token revoke <id>).
Create a new token if you need one; check your packages for versions you didn't publish.
private_key: Treat the key as public now. Make a new key pair (for SSH: ssh-keygen -t ed25519).
Replace the old public key everywhere it was trusted: servers' ~/.ssh/authorized_keys, GitHub deploy keys or SSH keys, and so on. Then remove the old one.
If it was Orion's updater signing key (.orion-signing): make a new one with the Tauri signer, update the GitHub Actions secret, and ship the new public key in the next release.
url_password: This is a password written inside a link (a name and password before an @ sign in an address).
Change that password on the service or database it belongs to.
Put the new password in .env and build the link from it at runtime.
generic: Work out which service this password, token or key belongs to (the line's name usually says, e.g. MYSQL_PASSWORD).
Change or regenerate it on that service so the old value stops working.
Put the new value in .env and read it from there in code.
